output:

**A Year of Remote Work: What We Actually Learned**

Last September we sent everyone home and told them to figure it out. A year later, the office lease is gone and so are most of our assumptions about how this team works best.

The biggest surprise was meetings. We cut our weekly meeting load by half in the first month, mostly out of necessity, and productivity went up, not down. Turns out a lot of what we called "alignment" was just people talking at each other because the conference room was free. Now we default to async updates in Slack and save live calls for decisions that actually need a room full of voices.

Onboarding got harder, then got fixed. Our first three remote hires spent their first two weeks lost, pinging five different people to piece together how anything worked. We wrote it down. A real onboarding doc, a buddy system, and a Slack channel just for new-hire questions turned that around within a quarter.

Trust matters more than hours. Nobody here clocks in or out. We stopped tracking time and started tracking output, and the engineers who used to stay late to look busy are now the ones shipping the most, because nobody's watching the clock anymore.

We also learned that some things just don't translate over video: debugging a gnarly production issue together, or the ten-minute hallway conversation that used to settle an argument in one sitting. We haven't solved that yet. We're not sure we will.
